summary:
MISSION ZERO: THE RED FRONTIER

MISSION ZERO is an interactive web-based Mars mission simulation that puts users in command of a fictional Martian habitat, ARES-01. We developed a platform where users make critical decisions to keep a crew alive while exploring the challenges of long-duration human missions beyond Earth.

The application brings together six interconnected systems: Mission Control, Life Support, Science Lab, Food Production, Emergency Response, and Mission Log. Users monitor essential resources, manage oxygen, water, energy, and food, analyze simulated Martian samples, operate a virtual greenhouse, and respond to emergencies. Their decisions influence the simulation, demonstrating how interconnected systems affect crew survival and mission success.

Inspired by NASA research and space exploration resources, MISSION ZERO transforms complex scientific and engineering challenges into an accessible, hands-on learning experience. It is important because it helps users understand the realities of sustaining human life on Mars, encourages scientific curiosity, and develops critical thinking, problem-solving, and resource-management skills.
details:
MISSION ZERO: THE RED FRONTIER

Team: YARUB SPACE

MISSION ZERO is an interactive, web-based Mars mission simulation that places users in command of a fictional Martian habitat called ARES-01. The project explores one of the greatest challenges of human space exploration: how to sustain human life on Mars while managing limited resources, scientific operations, and unexpected emergencies.

How It Works

Users take the role of a mission commander and make decisions that affect the habitat’s operations and crew survival. The platform brings together six interconnected modules:

  1. Mission Control: Monitor the mission status, crew, objectives, and available resources.
  2. Life Support: Manage oxygen, water, energy, and food while maintaining essential life-support systems.
  3. Science Lab: Investigate simulated Martian samples, explore their properties, and understand the scientific process.
  4. Food Production: Operate a virtual greenhouse and explore the challenges of growing food in a controlled environment.
  5. Emergency Response: Make decisions during simulated emergencies and evaluate their consequences.
  6. Mission Log & Science Data: Review mission decisions, track progress, and explore supporting scientific resources.

The modules are designed to demonstrate how decisions in one system can affect other systems and the overall success of the mission.

Benefits and Intended Impact

MISSION ZERO transforms complex space exploration concepts into an accessible, interactive learning experience. It helps users understand resource management, life-support systems, scientific investigation, sustainable food production, and emergency decision-making.

Our intended impact is to inspire interest in space science and STEM education, encourage critical thinking and problem-solving, and help students appreciate the engineering and scientific challenges involved in future human missions to Mars.

Tools and Technologies

The project is designed as a responsive web application for both computers and mobile devices. Our development approach uses:

  • React and Vite for the web application structure and development.
  • JavaScript / TypeScript for application logic and interactive systems.
  • Tailwind CSS for responsive interface styling.
  • Lucide Icons for interface symbols.
  • Recharts for resource monitoring and data visualization.
  • LocalStorage for saving simulation progress locally.
  • GitHub for source-code management.
  • Azure Static Web Apps as the intended deployment platform.

We also consulted space-science resources from NASA and the Canadian Space Agency, including NASA APIs, DONKI, the NASA Open Science Data Repository, Mars Trek, and educational resources about space food production.

Creativity and Innovation

The creative aspect of MISSION ZERO is its integrated mission-management approach. Instead of presenting Mars exploration as a collection of unrelated facts, it connects multiple systems into one simulated environment where users must consider the consequences of their decisions.

The project combines a mission-control-inspired interface, interactive resource management, simulated scientific investigations, and scenario-based emergency response to make learning more immersive and practical.

Factors Considered by Our Team

Our team considered scientific credibility, educational value, usability, accessibility, and technical feasibility. We designed the experience to work across different screen sizes and aimed to make complex concepts understandable without oversimplifying the challenges.

We also distinguished between real scientific references and simulated mission data. The habitat, crew operations, sample results, and resource scenarios are part of the educational simulation; they are not real-time measurements from Mars or an official NASA operational system.

MISSION ZERO is built around one central question: Can your decisions keep humanity alive on the Red Planet?
